projects.projectDescription: Free chicken tower defence on Steam: 15,000+ downloads and 2,500 leaderboard entries.

contentList.contentParagraph: A chicken tower defence game that finally answers "why did the chicken cross the road?" Throw wacky vehicles at the chicken hordes before they get to your corn, then fight your friends for the top of the leaderboards. Free on Steam for Windows and Mac, with no microtransactions.
Runner-up for Game Design at the IMIRT Irish Game Awards, at the Fís Games Summit in Dublin in April 2025.
With the rest of the night's winners.
Every vehicle has its own power.
Some chickens have abilities of their own.
Grab energy tokens to fuel your cars, and drop in heavy machinery with recharging ultimates.
Cash from each wave upgrades your vehicles, your ultimates and you.

Three of us made it: me as project manager and lead developer, with Anahat Mudgal and TheJackXBL. It's Unity and C#, with the Steamworks API for achievements, stats and leaderboards. It came out on 22 July 2024 and has been downloaded 15,000+ times, with 2,500+ leaderboard entries.

It began as our entry to GMTK Game Jam 2023. The theme was "roles reversed", so we flipped Crossy Road: instead of getting a chicken across the road, you stop them. It placed 263rd out of nearly 7,000 games, and we liked it enough to make it into a full game.

projects.tldr: A free game on Steam I made with two other devs. Downloaded 15,000+ times, and runner-up for Game Design at the 2025 IMIRT Irish Game Awards.

contentList.contentParagraph: Roadster Run was my final year project during my time at the National College of Ireland. It is a mobile phone game with motion controls and augmented reality (“AR”) functionality.

The gameplay involves a car that moves on a procedurally generated road, where the enemy will come to attack the player. The player’s car is controlled by rotating the phone left or right to change lanes. The player can also shoot at any oncoming enemy car to gain points and dispatch them.
The player can also customize their player car, which is reflected in the main game and AR functionality.
The AR functionality allows players to take images with their customized vehicles.
I have also created all art assets for the game in Blender.

projects.tldr: My final year project: a mobile game you steer by tilting your phone, with augmented reality.

projects.projectDescription: A one-month game jam FPS for HG-GJ, playable in your browser.
projects.tldr: My latest: an office FPS where you "repair" angry office machines with colour-coded blasters. Made in a month for a game jam.

contentList.contentParagraph: You're Morgan, a distracted office worker who's just been promoted to postman, IT technician and general repairman, all at once. Find the elusive Pepe Silvia and get his packages to him. The office equipment has turned on you, so you "repair" it with your blasters on the way.

contentList.contentTitle: Play it in your browser on itch.io

contentList.contentParagraph: Two blasters, one on each mouse button, and each lights up with the colour of its next bullet. Match the colour to the machine to build your combo, which boosts your damage and every bonus. The wrong colour costs you damage and a point of combo.
Red on a red machine cuts the Focus Time cooldown.<?>Green on a green machine drops health.<?>Blue on a blue machine drops a shield.
Press F when it's charged to slow everything down. While it's on, every hit does extra damage, whatever the colour. You also get a dodge that deflects shots, and a boomerang.

Made in a month for HG-GJ, HealthyGamerGG's first official game jam, and released on 1 October 2025. I did the programming and game design in Unity and C#: the movement, both blasters, the combo and RGB systems, the enemies and the package deliveries. Jamie Macleod did the 3D art and environments, and Jack Oades (DomHusk) did the music and sound. We're planning to turn it into a full game.

projects.mainPoints: Angular & TypeScript & Spring Boot & Java & MySQL & WebGL
projects.projectDescription: An Angular and Spring Boot portfolio with its content in a database, a WebGL ink background and bouncing windows.
projects.tldr: The site you're on. Everything on it lives in a database and is edited through the site itself, under a WebGL ink background and windows that bounce like a DVD screensaver.

contentList.contentParagraph: My portfolio, and the project I keep coming back to. Every project, job and write-up here is stored in MySQL and edited through the site itself, so I can add things without touching the code. The look is suminagashi, the Japanese art of floating black ink on water.

Spring Boot and Java, in the usual layers: controllers, services, and Spring Data JPA repositories over MySQL. Each project and job owns an ordered list of content blocks (text, image, video or link), and that list is what you see when you open a window. Lists come back newest first, deletes are soft, and logins use HTTP Basic with BCrypt passwords.

Angular. The background is a WebGL fragment shader: the lines are contours of a field around a few ink drops, folded by slowly drifting noise, and every line gets its own random weight.<?>The windows bounce around screen-sized spaces, off the edges and each other, and you can drag or throw them. Opening one grows it into the middle of the screen, and every page change plays an ink curtain that dissolves ring by ring.

It replaced my old jakedev.win. The Angular build sits in an S3 bucket behind Cloudflare, the Spring Boot API runs on EC2 and is reached through a Cloudflare Tunnel (no open ports and no certificates on the box), and MySQL lives on RDS with no public access. Before launch I gave the API a proper CORS setup, locked down the write endpoints, and moved its config into environment variables.

projects.projectDescription: A two-layer PyTorch network that reads MNIST handwritten digits, with an interactive visualizer in the browser.
projects.tldr: A neural network that reads handwritten digits, built step by step in PyTorch. Draw a digit in the browser and watch it flow through.

contentList.contentParagraph: A learn-by-building project: a small feed-forward network that classifies MNIST handwritten digits, put together one step at a time in PyTorch, with nearly every line commented to explain why. 784 pixels in, 128 hidden neurons, 10 digits out, and about 98% training accuracy after 5 epochs.

One HTML page that redoes the forward pass in JavaScript. Draw a digit and watch it flow through the network, switch between trained and random weights, click a hidden neuron to see its weights as a 28×28 heatmap, and step through a round of gradient descent with the maths worked out live.
Before training, a neuron's weights are noise. After, they turn into feature detectors: their spatial smoothness goes from about 0.0 to 0.63.
Fine-tuning can wreck a model in one step. A single update at a learning rate of 0.3 dropped test accuracy from 97.5% to about 10%. At 0.01 it fixes the misread digit for only a 0.3% hit.

projects.projectName: Games, Films and the Stock Market
projects.projectDescription: A college data analytics project in R testing whether hit games and films move their companies' share prices.
projects.tldr: Do hit games and films push up their company's share price? I tested it in R on Activision, Disney and Sony from 2006 to 2015. Mostly, no.

contentList.contentParagraph: My data analytics project at the National College of Ireland. I'd made a small profit investing on the idea that you can spot the next big game or film before the market does, so I put it to the test: do the biggest releases move a company's share price?

Ten years (2006 to 2015) of Activision (games), Disney (film) and Sony (both). Video game sales and IMDb film data from public datasets, daily share prices for each company, and Wikipedia's best-selling games and highest-grossing films, scraped with rvest.

R scripts that clean each dataset the same way, estimate yearly revenue from the products, and chart it against the number of releases. Then a set of functions takes any two trading days and works out the opening and closing price, the change, and the percentage difference, so I could check each big release against its quarter.

Big releases didn't reliably move the price. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 sold 25 million copies (about $1.25 billion by my estimate), yet Activision's shares fell 9.75% that quarter. A year later Black Ops lined up with a 13.2% rise. Sales and releases tracked each other closely, but the share price answered to much more than one product, and the 2009 recession didn't help. So I disproved my own hypothesis.

The other two built the map side in Mapbox GL JS and Bootstrap. My partner and I built the PHP and MySQL side: the account system (sign up, log in, sessions), photo uploads, and storing each user's markers as GeoJSON in the database so their map comes back the next time they log in.

projects.projectDescription: A button-mashing weightlifting game in Unity with brainCloud logins and leaderboards, made in about 15 hours.
projects.tldr: A button-mashing deadlift game that gets heavier every round, with online logins and leaderboards on brainCloud. Made in about 15 hours.

contentList.contentParagraph: Mash to lift the bar, and every round gets harder. I built it in Unity in about 15 hours to learn brainCloud, a game backend service.

You're signed in anonymously as soon as the game starts, and can add an email and password or sign into another account later. There are daily and all-time leaderboards, and the gravity and bonus multiplier come from global values on the server, so they can change without a new build. Two custom cloud scripts fetch every leaderboard in one call and post a score to several at once.

The first plan was several minigames played against each other in a lobby. brainCloud could do it, but not in the time I had, so I cut it down to one game done properly. By the end I really liked brainCloud's API and how open it is to building your own flows on top.

workExperiences.workDescription: SuperNimbus is a contracting company that provides back-end services for gaming projects. It was a client-facing role: I worked out what each project needed and built custom back-end services for it, hosted on AWS.

contentList.contentParagraph: I have worked on is USM's 'Catan Universe', by provideing custom RPCs, front end updates, and server stress testing automation. I have also worked on a up and coming multiplayer shooter Cathedral's 'The Bornless', providing authentication, user statistics, and in-app purchases.

One of the requirements for ‘The Bornless’ was to have full Twitch integration to allow users to claim in-game items from watching streams of the game. This system was fully integrated using the Playfab system for authentication and user management with the CloudScript functionality in JavaScript.<?>The system will gather all ‘Claimed’ status items from the attached Twitch account. Grant them to the player Inventory, and set them to ‘Fulfilled’ status. Of course, contacting multiple endpoints we need fallback mechanisms when there is a failure along the progress of the system, All failed Items are stored against the player's title data in a small JSON object. This object will be retried once the system is called, and be cleared when all items have been successfully granted to the player.

contentList.contentTitle: Economy Updates for granting Items (The Bornless)
contentList.contentParagraph: The Item grants system for ‘The Bornless’ backend project was previously implemented using the legacy Economy V1 with no fallback for any item failures, this could cause a major problem with the user not receiving items when they should if an endpoint failed. I was tasked with the implementation of a system that would store any failures and retry them at a later date. While I was developing this system I updated all instances of granting items to the new Economy V2 endpoints.<?>This system would store any failed item information in a new Dynamo DB table while it was attempting to grant items to each user. I managed to flesh out the common reasons why these items would fail and when recognized would attach it to the table, for example, if an item was attempted to be granted that was not created in the Econmy system on Playfab. A second socket endpoint was created on this back project to be called that would once again retry these failed items.

A policy change came through for the IOS store that directly affected the ‘Catan Universe’ application and its release of the next update. The solution for this was to add an info popup at the start of each new install of the application. Also, it was required that this popup would be translated into 6 other popular languages.

workExperiences.tldr: Custom game backends on AWS for client projects, including Catan Universe and The Bornless.

workExperiences.workDescription: At Mastercard I was a Back-End Software Engineer II, developing and maintaining the In Control for Commercial Payments (ICCP) platform, built with Java, Spring Framework and an Angular frontend. I worked mainly on the Smart Data project, a business-to-business solution for creating and controlling payments on virtual cards.

contentList.contentParagraph: I have made considerable contributions to developing web services for a health check system active in this platform with Java EE and Spring Framework, creating endpoints that will be consumed by both customers and internal teams.

The health check system was an endpoint that allowed internal and external customers to check the status of the ICCP application. This functionality was split into endpoints, shallow health returning a simple “status: UP” or “status: DOWN”, and deep health returning an in-depth analysis of all components relating to the ICCP application. These 2 endpoints would gather this information from cached values stored and logged by a background service every 30 seconds.<?>I was tasked with separating these two endpoints functionality, and making them have independent run times for caching and logging, 5 seconds for shallow, and 5 minutes for deep. Also, I was tasked with having the shallow endpoint return the cached value, while the deep endpoint would run the health check service independently and return the current status values.<?>I focused on the separation of the Heath check service into two by creating a DeepHealthService class and a ShallowHealthService class, also creating independent flags and variables to support this separation.<?>I used multithreading to create another scheduling task, that will be running DeepHealthService. I also created another cache store and logging functionality, for this value to be stored every 5 minutes. The previous thread handling the old implementation of health check service, was then repurposed to run the ShallowHealthService.<?>Finally, I pointed the deep endpoint that accessed the cached value, to now do an independent call to my DeepHealthService, and return this value to the end user.

There are many different applications that come together to make up the ICCP Platform. When each application contacts the other they have a passphrase type validation to verify that another application is from the MasterCard suite of applications. My Team, Team Vision was in charge of migrating this system to a new solution HashiCorp Vault. We were in charge of migrating CommercialAPI, PurchaseControlUI, CommercialApi Batch, and CommercialApi Report.<?>Mastercard has many different environments where applications are deployed and tested, Stage 1, Stage 2, Performance testing, MTF, MTF2. On top of these servers, we also need to migrate the servers based in the United States and India. We were provided with a ‘Cookbook solution’ by an alternative team on basic settings and procedures we should be doing to migrate servers.<?>As a Team, we had to develop a set of Instructions and Validations that needed to be carried out by members of Mastercard (BizOps) who have in-depth access to all server and Jenkins configurations. We created Pull Requests for each environment, that merged the new Hashi configurations on each of these specific servers. When these instructions were finalised, we needed to create a CRQ session with BizOps to carry out our steps and validations.<?>A major part I played in the Hashi Migration CRQ sessions with BizOps, was for the 8 servers in India. Mastercard cycles between an Active server set each weekend, 2 sets for 4 application. Due to our ICCP platform being a business solution, the best time to do this migration was on the weekend. We did the inactive set of 4 servers on Saturday, steps for migration, and validated the application functionality. That evening an alternative team performed with a cutover of making the migrated Hashi servers active, while also making the remaining 4 servers inactive. We then proceeded with the Hashi migration of the inactive servers on Sunday.

workExperiences.tldr: Java and Spring on the ICCP platform, mainly Smart Data: virtual cards for business payments.

workExperiences.workDescription: I was employed by Ergo, as a contractor for the Strategic Banking Corporation of Ireland (SBCI) to work on an emerging web application for the Irish Financial market, the SBCI customer hub. This application is a way for small businesses to access support for reduced-rate loans, allow for on-lenders to view and access these loan applications, and a system for the internal SBCI team to accept or deny these funding opportunities.

contentList.contentParagraph: There were several different loan schemes available for customers using the SBCI customer hub, where a user could select and fill out various pages to see if they were eligible for a reduced-rate loan. When a user selects a scheme it has a hard-coded set of eight pages that would need to be completed in order to apply for that loan. The introduction of the ‘Ukraine Credit Guarantee Scheme’ aimed at providing financial aid to businesses affected by the Ukraine crisis, the business needs required a new page progression to calculate if a customer was eligible for a subsidized loan.<?>I created a new component that allows the loan application to take in the scheme name and populate the application with the necessary components, decouple the stepper functionality from the to allow it to be populated with the passed-on information, and also allow for reused pages from other schemes to be populated with necessary legal text for it to be used in multiple scheme types.<?>This system has been continued, and used to support many different loan application schemes.

Before the release of the Customer Hub application, a major target for us was to restructure the design to fit all devices and be responsive to all screen sizes. When I joined the team I led the process with our UX designer to form a system using Flexbox CSS. Our goal was to keep the original design flow and philosophy while allowing smaller devices to be visible and intuitive.<?>I created a clear class-based system that allowed us to cut down on rewriting CSS code for each Angular component. We could then call clearly defined CSS classes and modifiers to allow each box of content to scale and restructure to allow the end user to access the app on any device.<?>Before release, we managed to restructure all of the customer-facing pages which include the login, loan application process pages, and the main menu with sub-menus. After release, we continued to bring the Flexbox CSS system to all other users including on lender and approvers.

workExperiences.tldr: Contracted to the SBCI, building the customer hub where small businesses apply for reduced-rate loans.
